subject: history
title: Henry VIII's Break with Rome
welcome_lead: The annulment that became a Reformation, 1527-47.
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on the Henrician Reformation and the royal supremacy.
final_note: You have severed England from papal jurisdiction.

concepts.def: Henry VIII's first wife (married 1509), whose failure to produce a male heir initiated the Great Matter.
Henry's second wife, married January 1533 and crowned in June; executed in May 1536.
Statute declaring Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England in place of the Pope.
1534 Act vesting the succession in Anne Boleyn's children and requiring oath; refused by More and Fisher.
1536 doctrinal statement showing moderate Protestant influence, reduced to three sacraments.
1539 statute reasserting conservative doctrine including transubstantiation; nicknamed 'whip with six strings'.

walkthroughs.body_html: Henry's marriage to Catherine produced only Mary. Convinced his union with his brother's widow was cursed by Leviticus, Henry sought annulment from 1527. Cardinal Wolsey failed; Pope Clement VII, captive of Charles V, refused. Henry turned to Cromwell, who used Parliament to declare papal authority foreign. Cranmer pronounced annulment on 23 May 1533; Anne was crowned on 1 June.

Submission of the Clergy (May 1532) subordinated convocation. Act in Restraint of Appeals (April 1533) ended appeals to Rome. Act of Supremacy (November 1534) made Henry Supreme Head. Act of First Fruits and Tenths (1534) seized papal revenues. The 1536 Dissolution of smaller monasteries dismantled centuries-old institutions; the 1539 Act of Six Articles, however, restored Catholic doctrine.

walkthroughs.h2: Was Henry's Reformation Catholic or Protestant?
walkthroughs.body_html: Henry rejected papal authority but retained Catholic doctrine on the mass, clerical celibacy and purgatory. The Bishops' Book (1537) and King's Book (1543) reflect cautious doctrinal change. Diarmaid MacCulloch describes a 'Reformation without doctrine', while Christopher Haigh's English Reformations (1993) stresses multiple, contested processes rather than a single shift toward Protestantism.
